items.t: Lawsuits Accuse 7 US Airlines Of Colluding To Raise Fares By Sharing Pricing Data
sum: Seven major US airlines — including the 'Big Four' American Airlines, Delta Air Lines, Southwest Airlines and United Airlines — have been accused of sharing confidential pricing data to avoid undercutting each other. Two proposed class action lawsuits claim the arrangement has helped keep domestic ticket prices artificially high, in violation of federal antitrust laws.

At the center of the allegations is an industry database that lets airlines track rivals' fares and quickly match price cuts, potentially removing the incentive for airlines to offer cheaper tickets in the first place. The lawsuits come amid growing scrutiny of airline pricing practices, with carriers facing questions over how exactly they determine their fares.

The larger of the two lawsuits was filed on November 4 in the US District Court for the Western District of Washington in Seattle. Along with American, Delta, Southwest and United, it named Alaska Airlines, Hawaiian Airlines and JetBlue as defendants, alongside the industry-owned organization Airline Tariff Publishing Company (ATPCO) and its subsidiary, 3Victors.

The suit describes ATPCO as "a highly sophisticated information exchange" that allows airlines to track one another’s pricing and "artificially inflate the cost of air travel." The alleged information sharing takes place through two products developed by 3Victors — Iris, which collects airline shopping and pricing data; and PriceEye, which allows airlines to compare prices and track competitors.

According to Courthouse News, airlines share their own 'shopping data' — including what routes and dates people searched for, and the fares offered — to Iris in exchange for access to PriceEye, which shows information on competitors' pricing. This effectively allows airlines to see when competitors are offering cheaper fares and respond quickly, preventing rivals from gaining an advantage by undercutting them.

Seattle-based law firm Hagens Berman said that the airlines using 3Victors' pricing tools account for around 80% of US domestic passengers. Speaking to The Seattle Times, the firm's managing partner, Steve Berman, explained that the tools let airlines see "in real time what everyone is charging for any route in the US." Berman said:

Delta Air Lines stock faces Heathrow terminal dispute with Virgin Atlantic
sum: Delta Air Lines is challenging Heathrow Airport Limited's plan to move its operation from Terminal 3 to Terminal 4 in 2028, separating it from joint-venture partner Virgin Atlantic. In a statement published on November 2, Chief Executive Ed Bastian called the decision short-sighted and bad for airline consumers, according to the Delta News Hub.

Delta says its more than decade-long co-location with Virgin Atlantic supports convenient connections, premium amenities and an expanded transatlantic network. The planned move would leave Virgin Atlantic in Terminal 3 while Delta operates from Terminal 4, potentially adding friction for passengers connecting between the two airlines.

Bastian said Delta would pursue all available remedies and urged Heathrow to reconsider. The statement did not specify a legal filing or other formal action, so the next step remains open. The proposed relocation is not an immediate schedule change and could still be modified before 2028.

sum: Oil is tumbling on U.S.-Iran peace talk hopes, and airline stocks are surging in response, but the carrier with the most to gain is also the one with the least room for error if diplomacy falls apart.

Airline stocks are rising as oil prices tumble on hopes that U.S.-Iran talks could ease supply fears, according to reports from The Wall Street Journal, CNBC and the Financial Times. JetBlue Airways (NASDAQ:JBLU) stock is at $3.18, up 11%, early in the session. Even after that jump, JetBlue stock is still down 30% year to date (YTD).

Jet fuel is one of the biggest costs any airline carries, so lower oil prices can quickly improve the profit outlook. JetBlue is the smallest of the five carriers. It is also the most fuel-sensitive in this group, and its shares are posting the largest gain in the group today.

WTI crude oil trades at $97.05 per barrel, down nearly 7% over the past 24 hours, on hopes for U.S.-Iran diplomacy. It comes after oil settled at $109.72 on October 23, so the move marks a retreat from multi-month highs. For JetBlue, the relief hits its most damaging cost.

JetBlue disclosed on October 26 that its Q3 2026 fuel costs surged 61% year over year (YoY) to $868 million at $3.91 per gallon. On an adjusted basis, the company lost $0.60 per share, missing the $0.55 consensus. Looking ahead, the company’s Q4 2026 guidance assumes fuel at $4.64 per gallon, so any lasting drop in oil could feed straight into its earnings.
United Airlines and American Airlines Ride the Same Fuel Relief

United Airlines Holdings (NASDAQ:UAL | UAL Price Prediction) stock is at $110.81, up 6%. sum: If you had put money into Delta Air Lines a year ago and simply left it alone, the outcome would look very different depending on which story you believed at the start. Holding Delta Air Lines over the past year would have returned 30.8%, including dividends. If the decision on 2025-10-21 hinged on flat capacity plans, a 10 year UPS MRO deal and worries about domestic softness and tariffs, which of those signals deserved more weight?
The easy part of this move is behind Delta Air Lines. Zero in on 33 high quality undervalued stocks for companies trading below our estimates.
The shares cost US$62.32 at the start of the period, and Delta Air Lines sat between two clean but very different stories about what came next.

On the optimistic side, the bullish narrative said the stock was worth a fair value of US$69.66. This price was implied by its own assumptions, leaning on a 3.4% revenue growth assumption, a 6.8% profit margin, and support from the 10-year UPS MRO agreement.

The bearish view put fair value at US$31. It was built around worries that domestic main cabin demand and potential tariffs on aircraft would pressure operating margins and leave rising non-fuel costs hard to absorb.

Record Q3 2026 revenue of US$20.2b supported the bullish idea that Delta Air Lines could keep demand and pricing power working, yet net income slipped to US$756m and net margin moved from 8.5% to 3.7%. Higher fuel costs and thinner profitability kept the profit-margin part of the optimistic case unproven, so the evidence cut both ways.
The useful takeaway is simple. When a thesis leans on margin assumptions, track net margin next to revenue in each report and see whether both stories move in the same direction.

Delta Air Lines Cuts 2026 Earnings Outlook: Time to Sell DAL Stock?
sum: Delta Air Lines DAL has lowered its full-year 2026 earnings guidance following disappointing third-quarter results released on Oct. 9, as surging fuel expenses and rising operating costs continue to pressure profitability. The airline now expects adjusted earnings of $5.10-$5.60 per share, down from its earlier projection of $6.50-$7.50.

In the third quarter of 2026, adjusted earnings of $1.72 per share missed the Zacks Consensus Estimate by 4.44%. Despite a 16% increase in adjusted revenues to $17.59 billion, escalating expenses weighed on margins. The combination of disappointing earnings and reduced guidance raises concerns about DAL's near-term prospects.

DAL's shares have gained 29% over the past year, outperforming the Zacks Transportation - Airline industry's 3.3% decline and the S&P 500's 18% growth. However, mounting cost pressures and weakening earnings expectations could challenge this momentum.

Surging Fuel Costs Pressure Margins: Delta's adjusted fuel expenses surged 62% year over year to $4.14 billion in the third quarter, as average fuel prices increased 60% to $3.61 per gallon. Consequently, adjusted operating income declined 2% to $1.66 billion, while adjusted operating margin contracted 170 basis points to 9.4%. Non-fuel expenses also increased 8%, reflecting higher crew and revenue-related costs.

The challenging fuel environment poses risks across the airline industry. United Airlines UAL and American Airlines AAL also operate in a fuel-sensitive industry, where higher energy prices can constrain profitability. Like DAL, both UAL and AAL face the broader challenge of balancing revenue growth with escalating operating expenses. We expect high fuel costs to hurt the third-quarter results of both United Airlines (scheduled to be released on Oct. 20) and American Airlines (scheduled to be released on Oct. 22).

Weakening Cash Flow and Financial Obligations: Delta generated $463 million in free cash flow during the September quarter, down from $833 million a year earlier. Higher capital expenditures and increased operating costs constrained cash generation. Although adjusted net debt declined $2.24 billion year over year to $13.35 billion, substantial financial obligations continue to limit flexibility.

Delta's Non-Main-Cabin Revenue Hits 61% in 2026 -- Why It Matters for Earnings
sum: The airline industry is notorious for its cyclicality. Traditionally, airlines like Delta Air Lines (DAL -0.17%) are seen as having strong pricing power when travel demand is high, only to suffer when demand wanes, as ticket prices decline while the airline continues to carry high fixed costs.
That said, Delta might not be as risky as you think, and the market may need to rethink how it values the company. Here's why.

Chief Commercial Officer Joe Esposito outlined on the second-quarter earnings call that "diverse revenue streams represented 61% of total revenue in the quarter, up 2 points over last year, with premium and loyalty revenue both up nearly 20%."

The 61% figure is impressive enough, and it makes sense to create an apples-to-apples comparison across the industry, as other airlines don't operate refineries (which is a low-margin business anyway). Still, I would argue that it underplays the issue.

By "diverse revenue streams," Esposito means Delta's non-main-cabin revenue. That's fair enough, but when calculating the 61%, Delta adjusts the revenue figure by stripping out its refinery sales to third parties. Esposito is referring to the bottom figure on the right side of the table, but including refinery sales increases the share of non-main-cabin revenue to 65.3%.

Sticking with my figure of 65.3%, it represents a significant increase over the full-year 2017 equivalent figure of 50%. Back then, main cabin revenue was 1.7 times Delta's premium cabin revenue, but as you can see above, Delta's premium cabin revenue exceeded main cabin revenue in the second quarter.

It's all part of a deliberate strategy to diversify Delta's revenue away from the extreme cyclicality of main cabin ticket revenue. As Esposito noted on the recent earnings call: "We're not growing Main Cabin seats. This is a multiyear, several years in a row, that we haven't grown this cabin. We won't be growing it next year either."

Archer Aviation vs. Delta Air Lines: Which Industrials Stock Is a Better Buy in 2026?
sum: Choosing between Archer Aviation (ACHR -6.07%) and Delta Air Lines (DAL -4.35%) requires weighing the speculative potential of urban air travel against the reliable cash flows of an established titan of the commercial aviation industry.

Archer Aviation is developing futuristic electric aircraft designed to transform how people move through congested cities. Delta Air Lines, meanwhile, provides traditional long-haul and regional travel services while generating significant cash flow from its global network. These companies represent different risk profiles, offering a choice between high-growth potential and the stability of a market leader.

Archer Aviation’s commercial strategy relies on a conditional purchase agreement with United Airlines for up to $1.5 billion worth of its Midnight aircraft. Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business, though it also provides a massive potential order backlog for the future. The company also collaborates with the U.S. Air Force and has a manufacturing relationship with Stellantis to support high-volume production of its electric vertical takeoff-and-landing vehicles.

In FY 2025, Archer Aviation generated revenue of approximately $300,000 as it began navigating its early development and testing milestones. During the same period, the company reported a net loss of nearly $618.2 million, which is common for companies in the pre-commercial phase of aerospace engineering. This net loss reflects the significant capital required for research, development, and the pursuit of necessary flight certifications.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, Archer Aviation had a debt-to-equity ratio of roughly 0.1x, which measures its total debt obligations relative to its shareholder equity. The current ratio, a metric used to determine if a company can cover its short-term debts with short-term assets, was approximately 19.9x. Free cash flow for the year was nearly negative $511.7 million, representing the cash used in operations and equipment purchases as the company funds its growth.
Delta Air Lines operates a massive global network serving more than 300 destinations across six continents and is a prominent name among industrial stocks.

items.t: Delta's Profits vs. GE's Premiums: Is the Market Mispricing These 2 Stocks?
sum: The valuation discrepancy between GE Aerospace (GE +1.95%) and Delta Air Lines (DAL +1.75%) speaks volumes about how investors view the commercial aerospace industry. While that view has historical precedent, I think the industry has changed, and the market is at least mispricing Delta Air Lines.
How the market thinks about the commercial aerospace industry

The chart below goes a long way to explaining matters. Network airlines like Delta and United Airlines are trading on very attractive valuations relative to aerospace equipment supplier GE Aerospace. The interesting thing is that GE, and its joint venture with Safran, CFM International, are leading players in the commercial engine market that powers airlines' flight departures, so why the valuation discrepancy between the main users of aircraft engines and the key supplier of them?

The answer lies in the traditional cyclicality of commercial airlines and their historical inability to generate the return on invested capital necessary to cover their cost of capital, due to the industry's continuous boom-and-bust cycles. When the going is good, airlines traditionally rush to build capacity and expand routes, only to eventually walk into a slowdown, burdened with relatively high fixed costs that push them to maintain capacity while hoping for a rebound.

Unfortunately, these dynamics have led to wild swings in profitability. While you might think the capital markets would be wary of the industry, the reality is that the debt is backed by credible assets: the aircraft.

As such, it's traditionally been a great market for bondholders and equipment suppliers, who benefit from the transfer of capital from bond and equity markets to airline industry assets, but a lousy one for equity holders. Warren Buffett himself is on record decrying investing in airlines, although interestingly, Berkshire Hathaway has taken a stake in Delta since Buffett handed over control to Greg Abel.

Samsung Electronics tanked 10% as investors looked beyond the South Korean electronics giant'sforecast of a 19-fold jump in second-quarter earnings, with results failing to alleviate concerns about the sustainability of the AI-driven chip boom.
"Samsung's decline suggests the AI trade is becoming increasingly valuation-sensitive," said Glenn Yin, director of research at ACCM.

The market needs evidence that AI spending and earnings growth can keep accelerating, otherwise, tech-heavy Asian markets, where performance has grown increasingly concentrated in a handful of AI-related companies, could face a rapid de-rating, Yin added.

Delta Air Lines Q2 2026 Earnings Preview — July 10, Street Expects $1.48 EPS
sum: Wall Street expects a sharp earnings decline when Delta Air Lines reports second-quarter results on July 10 during market hours. The consensus among 17 analysts calls for earnings per share of $1.48 on revenue of $18.78B. The EPS estimate range spans $1.25 to $1.63, while revenue estimates range from $17.52B to $19.57B, reflecting meaningful uncertainty about the quarter’s outcome.

Analyst sentiment has shifted dramatically over the past three months. While estimates have ticked up 2.1% over the past 30 days from $1.45, the 90-day picture tells a more concerning story: EPS estimates have plunged 26.4% from $2.01 three months ago. This substantial downward revision suggests analysts have encountered deteriorating fundamentals—whether from pricing pressure, capacity decisions, or cost inflation—that have forced a meaningful reset of expectations heading into the print.

The year-over-year comparison reveals a stark reversal in profitability. Consensus EPS of $1.48 implies a decline of 29.5% from the year-ago quarter’s $2.10 per share, a dramatic contraction that signals either margin compression or higher share count dilution. Revenue, by contrast, is expected to grow 12.8% from last year’s $16.65B, creating a scissors effect where top-line growth substantially outpaces bottom-line performance. In the year-ago quarter, Delta generated net income of $1.37B on an 8.2% net margin, operating income of $2.10B with a 12.6% operating margin. If revenue grows as expected while earnings collapse, investors should scrutinize whether cost pressures—fuel, labor, or otherwise—are eroding the operating leverage that typically defines airline economics during strong demand periods.

The prior quarter provides limited guidance context. Management issued first-quarter 2026 guidance calling for adjusted EPS in a range of $1.00 to $1.50. With the current quarter consensus at $1.48, analysts are essentially modeling performance at the high end of that prior outlook, though the wide dispersion of individual estimates suggests continued debate about the trajectory.

Delta has recently been reliable in meeting or exceeding expectations. The company beat estimates in one of the last one quarters reported, a 100% beat rate that suggests management has maintained credibility with the Street.
